Where it began

Ranjitsinhji came into the world on 10 September 1872, in the village of Sadodar in western India's state of Nawanagar. He went to the Rajkumar College in Rajkot, a school run on English public-school lines, where he captained the cricket side from 1884 to 1888. At the time he preferred tennis.

In 1888 he sailed for England and went up to Trinity College, Cambridge. A trip to watch the touring Australians play Surrey that year seems to have lit the spark. He set about improving his batting in earnest, working in the nets with Daniel Hayward, and in 1893 he made his first-class bow for the university and won his Blue. His friends found his full name a mouthful, tried calling him Smith, and settled on Ranji.

The player

He joined Sussex, hit 150 in his very first match for them, and became the county's great draw. He played 15 Tests for England between 1896 and 1902, scoring 989 runs at 44.95 with two hundreds and six fifties.

His Test debut, against Australia in July 1896, was a marvel. England were following on, and on the final morning he made 113 runs before lunch on the way to 154 not out. That season he scored 2,780 first-class runs, passing W. G. Grace's record. In Australia in 1897–98 he made 175 in the first Test, then England's highest Test score. In 1899 he took over the Sussex captaincy and became the first man to reach 3,000 runs in a first-class summer.

What made him special

Before him, batsmen mostly went forward and played to the off side. Ranji went back, waited, and used his quick eye and wrists to send the ball wherever he wished. His name is tied above all to the leg glance. He made the shot popular, and he may well have been its inventor. Part of it grew from a net session in which his right leg was tied to the ground to stop him backing away. Most coaches would not recommend the method, but it worked.

Crowds at Brighton could not quite work out how he did it. Opposing captains packed the leg side to stop him, so he became a fine driver of the ball as well.

Away from the middle

In 1907 he became ruler of Nawanagar, his home state, and held that position until 1933. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and was knighted twice over, in the Order of the Indian Empire and the Order of the British Empire. With C. B. Fry, his friend and Sussex team-mate, he produced The Jubilee Book of Cricket in 1897. His nephew Duleepsinhji followed him to Cambridge, Sussex and England. He died in 1933.

And finally

India's national first-class championship, first played in 1935, is called the Ranji Trophy in his honour. Not many cricketers get a trophy named after them. Fewer get one named after their nickname.
